packages.name: morgan
packages.synopsis: Package morgan is an HTTP request logger middleware for net/http, ported from the Node.js expressjs/morgan library (the request logger most commonly seen mounted on Express applications).
packages.doc:
Package morgan is an HTTP request logger middleware for net/http, ported from
the Node.js expressjs/morgan library (the request logger most commonly seen
mounted on Express applications). Like its namesake, morgan produces one
access-log line per HTTP request and derives the fields of that line by
expanding named tokens — :method, :url, :status, :response-time and so on —
against the request and the response it observed. The goal of the port is
behavioural parity: the same format names, the same token syntax, and the
same Common Log Format output, expressed idiomatically in Go and depending
only on the standard library.

Use morgan when you want structured, human- or machine-readable access logs
for an HTTP service without adopting a heavier logging framework. It answers
the operational questions an access log exists to answer — who called what,
when, with which method and path, what status came back, how large the
response was, and how long it took — and it does so uniformly for every
handler it wraps. Typical uses are request auditing, latency spot-checks,
feeding an existing log pipeline, or simply having readable local output
during development.

The central entry point is New, which wraps any http.Handler and returns a
new http.Handler that logs each request as it passes through. Internally New
substitutes a small responseRecorder for the real http.ResponseWriter so that
the status code, the response headers (and therefore the reported content
length), and the moment headers are flushed can be captured without the
wrapped handler being aware of it. Timing is measured around the call to the
inner handler, giving both :response-time (arrival to headers written) and
:total-time (arrival to fully written). Once the handler returns, the
collected values are assembled into a Log and the active FormatFunc renders
the final line.

Output is controlled by a Format, which is either a predefined constant or a
raw format string. The predefined formats mirror Node morgan exactly:
Combined (Apache combined log format, the fullest line, including referrer
and user agent), Common (Apache common log format), Dev (concise output whose
:status is colored by response class — green 2xx, cyan 3xx, yellow 4xx, red
5xx — for terminal use), Short (like common plus response time and without
the bracketed date), and Tiny (the minimal method/url/status/length/time
line). This port additionally offers JSON, which emits one JSON object per
request. Raw format strings use :token and :token[arg] placeholders. Fifteen tokens are
predefined — among them :method, :url, :status, :response-time, :total-time,
:remote-addr, :remote-user, :referrer, :user-agent, :http-version, :pid and
:incoming, plus the argument-taking :date[clf|iso|web], :req[header] and
:res[header] — and a missing or empty token value renders as "-". Formats are
compiled into a FormatFunc by Compile, tokens are resolved from a live
registry at render time, and the token set can be extended at runtime with
Token. Named formats can be added with RegisterFormat (a format string) or
RegisterFormatFunc (a FormatFunc).

Behaviour beyond the format is configured through Config, and its options are
deliberately close to the Node API. Config.Stream sets the destination writer
(the analogue of morgan's stream option, defaulting to os.Stdout);
Config.Buffer enables interval-based buffered flushing (morgan's buffer
option); Config.Immediate writes the line on request arrival rather than on
response completion, trading away response fields such as status and length
for a guarantee the request is logged even if the handler never returns; and
Config.Skip is the equivalent of morgan's skip function, receiving the
request and the observed status and returning true to suppress the line.
Config.TrustProxy has no Node counterpart and is the security-relevant
exception: X-Forwarded-For and X-Forwarded-Proto are client-settable on a
direct connection, so :remote-addr and :protocol ignore them unless it is
enabled — the same default Express applies through its "trust proxy" setting.
Custom tokens (Token) and the compiled-format machinery (Compile, FormatFunc)
round out the parity. The most notable difference from the Node library is
naturally the type system: tokens receive a strongly typed Log rather than
loosely typed request/response objects, and Go's io.Writer stands in for a
Node writable stream.

Two concerns that do not arise in Node are handled here. Writes to the
destination stream are serialised, so lines from concurrently served requests
can never interleave and an unsynchronised io.Writer is safe to supply. And the
http.ResponseWriter the middleware substitutes exposes exactly the optional
interfaces the real writer implements — http.Flusher, http.Hijacker,
http.Pusher, io.ReaderFrom — plus Unwrap for http.NewResponseController, so
streaming responses, WebSocket upgrades, HTTP/2 push and sendfile all keep
working, and handlers that feature-detect still get a truthful answer.

See API-DEVIATIONS.md for the complete list of intentional differences from
the Node library.

types.name: Config
types.doc: Config holds the options for a morgan middleware instance.

types.name: Format
types.doc: Format is a predefined or custom log format string. Tokens use :name or :name[arg] syntax.

types.name: FormatFunc
types.signature: type FormatFunc func(r *http.Request, log Log) string
types.doc:
FormatFunc is a compiled format function that renders a single log line.
An empty return value signals that the line should be skipped.

funcs.name: Compile
funcs.doc:
Compile compiles a format string into a FormatFunc. Tokens are resolved from
the live registry at render time, so tokens registered after Compile is called
are still visible.

Token syntax: :name or :name[arg].

types.name: IP
types.doc: IP represents an IP address as a slice of bytes.

methods.name: String
methods.doc:
String returns the textual form of the IP address, or "<nil>" when the
address is empty. It matches the formatting of net.IP.String.

types.name: Log
types.doc: Log holds all token values captured for a single HTTP request/response cycle.

funcs.name: FromRequest
funcs.signature: func FromRequest(r *http.Request, status int, responseTime, totalTime time.Duration) Log
funcs.doc:
FromRequest populates a Log from an incoming HTTP request and timing
information. RESPONSE_HEADERS, RESPONSE_SIZE and RESPONSE_STREAMED must be set
by the caller after the handler runs.

The remote address is taken from r.RemoteAddr only. X-Forwarded-For is
deliberately ignored, because any client on a direct connection can set that
header and thereby forge the address written to the access log. Use
FromRequestTrustProxy (or Config.TrustProxy) when — and only when — every
request is known to arrive through a reverse proxy that overwrites the header.
This matches Express, where morgan's :remote-addr reads req.ip and the
"trust proxy" setting defaults to off.

funcs.name: FromRequestTrustProxy
funcs.signature: func FromRequestTrustProxy(r *http.Request, status int, responseTime, totalTime time.Duration) Log
funcs.doc:
FromRequestTrustProxy is FromRequest with proxy headers trusted: the left-most
entry of X-Forwarded-For supplies :remote-addr and X-Forwarded-Proto supplies
:protocol. Only call it for traffic that cannot reach the process without
passing through a proxy you control; otherwise a client can choose the address
that appears in the log.

methods.name: String
methods.doc: String returns the log line in Combined format.

types.name: SkipFunc
types.signature: type SkipFunc func(r *http.Request, status int) bool
types.doc:
SkipFunc decides whether the log line for a request/response pair should be
suppressed. It has the same signature as Config.Skip and any SkipFunc may be
assigned directly to that field.

Returning true suppresses the line; returning false logs it. This mirrors the
skip option of the Node.js morgan library, whose README documents the same
"return true to skip" convention.

funcs.name: CombineSkips
funcs.doc:
CombineSkips returns a SkipFunc that suppresses logging when any of the given
SkipFuncs would suppress it (a logical OR). Nil entries are ignored. Calling
CombineSkips with no functions returns a SkipFunc that never skips.

It lets several independent policies be composed, for example:

	Skip: morgan.CombineSkips(
	    morgan.SkipPaths("/healthz"),
	    morgan.SkipStatusBelow(400),
	)

funcs.name: SkipPaths
funcs.doc:
SkipPaths returns a SkipFunc that suppresses logging for any request whose URL
path exactly matches one of the given paths. It is the standard way to keep
health-check and readiness endpoints (for example "/healthz" or "/metrics")
out of an access log.

Matching is performed against r.URL.Path only; query strings are ignored. A nil
request never matches.

funcs.name: SkipStatusBelow
funcs.doc:
SkipStatusBelow returns a SkipFunc that suppresses logging whenever the
response status code is below min. It is the Go form of morgan's canonical
"only log errors" example, SkipStatusBelow(400), which skips every 1xx/2xx/3xx
response and logs only 4xx and 5xx.

A status of 0 (no response written, e.g. under Config.Immediate) is treated as
below any positive min and is therefore skipped.

funcs.name: SkipStatusBetween
funcs.doc:
SkipStatusBetween returns a SkipFunc that suppresses logging whenever the
response status code is within the inclusive range [lo, hi]. It is useful for
silencing an uninteresting band of statuses, for example SkipStatusBetween(200,
399) to log only redirects-and-errors-excluded... i.e. only 1xx, 4xx and 5xx.

funcs.name: SkipUserAgents
funcs.doc:
SkipUserAgents returns a SkipFunc that suppresses logging for any request whose
User-Agent header contains one of the given case-insensitive substrings. It is
commonly used to drop noise from uptime monitors, load-balancer probes and
crawlers, for example SkipUserAgents("kube-probe", "ELB-HealthChecker").

An empty substring is ignored so that it never matches every request.

types.name: TokenFunc
types.signature: type TokenFunc func(r *http.Request, log Log, args ...string) string
types.doc:
TokenFunc is the callback signature for a token handler. It receives the original
request, the populated Log, and any bracket arguments (e.g. "clf" from :date[clf]),
and returns the string to render at that position in the log line.

funcs.name: Clfdate
funcs.doc:
Clfdate formats t in Common Log Format, for example "27/Nov/2024:06:21:42
+0000". The value is always expressed in UTC with a fixed +0000 offset, exactly
matching the :date[clf] token and the Node.js morgan clfdate helper. It is
exported so callers building custom format functions can reuse the identical
timestamp rendering.

funcs.name: ClientIP
funcs.doc:
ClientIP resolves the client address for a request the way the :remote-addr
token does by default: the host portion of r.RemoteAddr, with any port
stripped. An empty string is returned for a nil request.

X-Forwarded-For is NOT consulted. That header is attacker-controlled on any
connection that did not in fact traverse a reverse proxy, so honouring it
unconditionally would let a client choose the address recorded in the access
log — and, by extension, poison anything keyed off that address such as abuse
detection or rate limiting. Use ClientIPTrustProxy (or Config.TrustProxy) when
the deployment guarantees a proxy that overwrites the header. Express takes the
same position with its "trust proxy" setting, which is off by default.

funcs.name: ClientIPTrustProxy
funcs.doc:
ClientIPTrustProxy resolves the client address honouring X-Forwarded-For: the
left-most (client-most) entry of that header is returned when it is present,
otherwise the host portion of r.RemoteAddr.

Only use it when every request necessarily arrives through a proxy you control
that replaces any client-supplied X-Forwarded-For; otherwise the returned
address is whatever the caller chose to claim.

funcs.name: FormatDuration
funcs.signature: func FormatDuration(d time.Duration, digits int) string
funcs.doc: FormatDuration formats a duration as milliseconds with the given number of decimal digits.

funcs.name: New
funcs.signature: func New(next http.Handler, format Format, cfg Config) http.Handler
funcs.doc:
New returns an http.Handler middleware that logs each request using the given
format and configuration. format may be a named format ("combined", "dev", …)
or a raw format string with :token syntax.

Example:

	mux := http.NewServeMux()
	http.ListenAndServe(":8080", morgan.New(mux, morgan.Dev, morgan.Config{}))

funcs.name: RegisterFormat
funcs.doc:
RegisterFormat registers a named format string.
Overwrites any existing format with the same name.

funcs.name: RegisterFormatFunc
funcs.doc:
RegisterFormatFunc registers a named format function.
Overwrites any existing format with the same name.

funcs.name: RequestProtocol
funcs.doc:
RequestProtocol reports the scheme under which a request was received: "https"
when the connection is TLS-terminated (r.TLS != nil), and "http" otherwise. It
backs the :protocol token.

X-Forwarded-Proto is NOT consulted, for the same reason ClientIP ignores
X-Forwarded-For: a direct client can set it freely. Use
RequestProtocolTrustProxy (or Config.TrustProxy) behind a proxy you control.

funcs.name: RequestProtocolTrustProxy
funcs.doc:
RequestProtocolTrustProxy reports the request scheme honouring
X-Forwarded-Proto, falling back to r.TLS. It mirrors Express req.protocol with
"trust proxy" enabled, and carries the same requirement: only enable it when a
proxy you control overwrites the header on every request.

funcs.name: RequestURL
funcs.doc:
RequestURL returns the request target rendered exactly as the :url token: the
original, still percent-encoded request target, which is what Node morgan logs
via req.originalUrl. A nil request or nil URL yields an empty string. It lets
custom format functions reproduce morgan's :url without duplicating the
assembly logic.

The raw target is used rather than the decoded r.URL.Path on purpose. Go
decodes percent escapes into r.URL.Path, so a request for "/a%0Aevil" would
otherwise put a real newline into the log line and let any client forge an
additional, fully attacker-controlled log record. Node has no such exposure
because req.originalUrl is never decoded, so keeping the encoded form is both
the safe choice and the faithful one.

funcs.name: StatusCategory
funcs.doc:
StatusCategory classifies an HTTP status code into its RFC 7231 response class
and returns a lowercase, hyphenated label:

	1xx -> "informational"
	2xx -> "success"
	3xx -> "redirect"
	4xx -> "client-error"
	5xx -> "server-error"

A status of 0 (no response written) or any code outside the 100-599 range
returns "unknown". This mirrors the response-class reasoning the dev format
uses to colour the status code, exposed for use in custom tokens and Skip
functions.

funcs.name: StatusColorCode
funcs.doc:
StatusColorCode returns the ANSI Select Graphic Rendition (SGR) colour code the
dev format applies to a status of the given class:

	5xx -> 31 (red)
	4xx -> 33 (yellow)
	3xx -> 36 (cyan)
	2xx -> 32 (green)
	otherwise -> 0 (no colour)

The returned value is the numeric parameter of an ESC[<code>m sequence, so a
coloured status can be rendered as "\x1b[" + strconv.Itoa(StatusColorCode(s)) +
"m". It reproduces exactly the palette documented for morgan.Dev.

funcs.name: Token

examples.name: Clfdate
examples.doc:
ExampleClfdate renders a timestamp exactly as :date[clf] does, which is what a
hand-written FormatFunc needs in order to stay byte-compatible with the
combined and common formats. The value is always UTC with a literal +0000
offset, matching the Node implementation.

examples.name: ClientIP
examples.code:
package main

import (
	"fmt"
	"net/http"
	"net/http/httptest"

	"github.com/malcolmston/morgan"
)

func main() {
	r := httptest.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, "/search?q=go&page=2", nil)
	r.RemoteAddr = "198.51.100.4:44321"
	r.Header.Set("X-Forwarded-For", "203.0.113.9, 10.0.0.1")

	fmt.Println(morgan.ClientIP(r))           // header ignored: not trusted
	fmt.Println(morgan.ClientIPTrustProxy(r)) // left-most entry of the header
	fmt.Println(morgan.RequestURL(r))         // exactly what :url renders
	fmt.Println(morgan.RequestProtocol(r))    // from r.TLS only
	fmt.Println(morgan.StatusCategory(503))   // response class label
	fmt.Println(morgan.StatusColorCode(503))  // ANSI colour the dev format uses
}
examples.doc:
ExampleClientIP shows the request helpers a custom token or format function can
reuse instead of reimplementing morgan's own resolution rules.

examples.name: New
examples.doc:
ExampleNew demonstrates the most common use of the package: wrapping an
existing http.Handler with a predefined format. Here the Tiny format is used,
which renders the method, URL, status, response content length and response
time. The middleware is driven with an httptest request and recorder so the
example is fully self-contained and does not need a live network listener.
Log output is redirected into a bytes buffer via Config.Stream instead of the
default os.Stdout so the test can inspect it. The takeaway is that a single
call to New turns any handler into a logged handler without changing the
handler itself. Because the Tiny format includes a non-deterministic
response-time value, the example asserts only that a stable substring is
present rather than printing the whole line.

examples.name: RegisterFormat
examples.doc:
ExampleRegisterFormat registers a format string under a name so that name can
be passed to New wherever a predefined format like morgan.Tiny would go. This
mirrors morgan.format(name, string) in the Node library and is the tidiest way
to share one house format across several services.

examples.name: RegisterFormatFunc
examples.doc:
ExampleRegisterFormatFunc registers a Go function instead of a format string,
which is the escape hatch for output that a :token template cannot express —
here a key=value rendering that varies with the status class. It mirrors
morgan.format(name, fn) in the Node library.

examples.name: Token
examples.doc:
ExampleToken shows how to extend morgan with a custom token and then use that
token inside a raw format string. A token named "app-version" is registered
with Token; its handler ignores the request and returns a fixed string, but a
real handler could read anything from the request or Log. The format string
combines the built-in :method and :url tokens with the new :app-version
token, and New compiles it because the string is not a registered format
name. Tokens are resolved from the live registry at render time, so
registering the token before the request is served is sufficient. The
takeaway is that any per-request value you can compute can become a first
class token; because this format contains no timing or date tokens, its
output is deterministic and can be asserted exactly.

examples.name: Token (args)
examples.doc:
ExampleToken_args shows a token that takes a bracket argument, the same
mechanism :date[clf] and :req[header] use. The argument is passed through as
the first variadic parameter.

examples.name: Config (buffer)
examples.output:
written before the interval elapses: false
GET /a 200
GET /b 200
examples.doc:
ExampleConfig_buffer shows the buffer option, which batches log lines in
memory and flushes them to the stream on a fixed interval instead of writing
each line straight through. It trades a small amount of latency for far fewer
syscalls on a busy server.

examples.name: Config (immediate)
examples.doc:
ExampleConfig_immediate shows the immediate option: the line is written when
the request arrives rather than when the response completes. That guarantees
the request is recorded even if the handler hangs or the process dies, at the
cost of every response-derived field — :status, :res[...], :response-time and
:total-time all render as a dash, because none of them exists yet.

examples.name: Config (skip)
examples.output:
logged after success: false
has 404 line: true
examples.doc:
ExampleConfig_skip demonstrates directing output to a custom io.Writer while
suppressing routine requests with a Skip function. The Skip callback receives
the request and the observed status code and returns true to drop the line,
so returning status < 400 here means only client and server errors are
logged. Two requests are driven through the same middleware: a successful one
that Skip suppresses, and a not-found one that is kept. The example inspects
the buffer after each request to show the filtering taking effect. The
takeaway is that Config.Stream and Config.Skip together let you send access
logs anywhere an io.Writer can reach while logging only the requests you care
about, mirroring the stream and skip options of the Node morgan middleware.

examples.name: Config (trustProxy)
examples.doc:
ExampleConfig_trustProxy shows the opt-in required before :remote-addr will
believe X-Forwarded-For. The header is set by the client on a direct
connection, so morgan ignores it by default and reports the real peer; enabling
TrustProxy is only correct when a reverse proxy you control overwrites the
header on every request.

examples.name: Format (predefined)
examples.doc:
ExampleFormat_predefined renders each predefined format against one fixed Log
so the shape of every line can be compared side by side without running a
server. A real request would supply these fields from FromRequest.

examples.name: Compile
examples.doc:
ExampleCompile shows that a format string can be parsed once into a reusable
FormatFunc and then rendered against any Log. This is what New does
internally, and it is the entry point to use when you want to build log lines
yourself — inside a custom FormatFunc, a test, or a non-HTTP context.
Compile resolves tokens from the live registry at render time, so a token
registered after the call is still picked up.

examples.name: CombineSkips
examples.doc:
ExampleCombineSkips layers several independent suppression policies with a
logical OR: probe endpoints and probe user-agents are dropped by path and by
User-Agent, and so is anything that succeeded, leaving only real failures in
the access log.
